newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Odds seen shortening for timely EMU launch.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Odds seen shortening for timely EMU launch.

text.p: The odds for Europe's single currency starting on time in 1999 have improved over the past month and optimism among commentators has rarely been higher for a core launch group of six countries, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

An exclusive poll of the views of 49 economists and political analysts across Europe gave an average likelihood of 82 percent that European economic and monetary union (EMU) would start on time in January 1999, compared with an average rating of 80 percent in April.
All 49 said they expected a core group of Austria, France, Germany and the Benelux countries to launch EMU.

Finland and Ireland were selected as by far the strongest also-rans -- all but two of the contributors said they expected Ireland to be in the first wave, while 44 out of the 49 participants selected Finland.
Asked the percentage likelihood of each country joining in the first wave, Ireland's chances were rated on average at 95 percent and Finland's at 90 percent.

The overall optimism reflected in the poll, conducted between May 7 and 12, is among the highest recorded since the Reuters survey started last October, but falls slightly short of the 86 percent average prediction for an on-time EMU launch posted in December, shortly after the Dublin summit meeting of European leaders.
That summit overcame a major hurdle, agreeing a stability pact to enforce fiscal discipline on EMU members.

This month's election of a Labour government in Britain, while more pro-European than its Conservative predecessor, is unlikely to promote the country into the ranks of the single currency club's first group, the survey found.
None of the respondents expected Britain to join from the start, and its chances of being in the first wave were rated on average at only 20 percent.
But Labour's sweeping reforms of the Bank of England, giving the central bank independence to set interest rates, were perceived as speeding Britain's eventual entry.
Most analysts anticipated a delay beyond 1999 of Britain's entry into EMU, and the average lag shortened to two years in this survey from three years last month.

The bullish mood for Britain was reflected on Tuesday by Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, who said the moves to grant the Bank of England operational leeway made it "less unlikely" that Britain would be among the first group of nations to join a single currency.
Italy's fervent wish to join EMU's first wave was greeted once again by contributors in the Reuters survey with a high degree of scepticism.

Only seven of the contributors thought that the Italians would make it from the start, and the average chance of it being a founder member was put at 40 percent, with those expecting a delay anticipating on average that Italy would have to wait two years before joining.

Italy's chances of joining the single currency from the start were cast further into doubt on Monday when EU finance ministers approved a sharply worded report saying that Rome was falling short in efforts to get its economy in order.
The ministers were far more complimentary about Spain and Portugal, whose efforts to catch up with the EU's northern economies were praised.
The Reuters poll reflected the bullish mood for Iberia.

A total of 26 and 27 contributors said they thought Portugal and Spain respectively would make it into EMU's first wave. The average likelihood that they would be founder members of the euro group was 65 percent in the poll, with those expecting a delay putting the wait for entry at an average of 12 months.

The perceived chances of founder membership for Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Greece were put at practically zero. Greece is struggling to get its economy into shape while the major obstacle for the other three was seen as political.

In Denmark and Sweden, constitutional obstacles and public opinion may prompt a move against early membership, the analysts said, while Britain's new government under Tony Blair, while less Euro-sceptic than its Conservative predecessor, would not have time to prepare Britain for the first wave.
